name: Colloquy of Regensburg
datesNote: 1541. Peter Faber's letter of 12 March, as the MHSI editors quote it, says the legate entered the city that afternoon. Sarpi says the Diet began in March and its first business on 5 April. Calvin dates the naming of the six speakers to 20 April. His letter of 11 May reports the agreement on justification. Sarpi dates the recess, the Diet's closing decree, to 28 July. Calvin's letter of 3 August says the Diet had ended.
teaser: Regensburg, 1541. Inside the emperor's Diet, three Catholic and three Protestant theologians sought agreement. They reached a formula on justification but split on the Lord's Supper, and the Diet referred everything to a council.
knownFor: The talks at the imperial Diet of 1541 where Catholic and Protestant theologians reached a formula on justification, then broke down over the Lord's Supper.
issue: The emperor's hope. Sarpi says Charles V came to the Diet in person, hoping to end all discord and unite religion. He had asked the pope for a legate with ample authority.
The emperor's pressures. Calvin, writing from the city, says his mind was 'altogether turned to peace'. He feared the Turk, and an uncertain peace or open war with the king of France.
The Protestant aim. Calvin says they expected no lasting peace without 'a settled agreement in religion'. They would urge the estates to take the work in hand.

The plan. Sarpi and Pallavicino say the emperor proposed that a few godly and learned men from each side confer on the disputes. Pallavicino adds the emperor's proviso, 'always saving' the decision and constitution of Augsburg.
Rome's view, in Paul III's bull of 1542. Treating reunion in the diets 'seemed only adapted to excite greater discord'. So the pope turned back to a general council.
What came before. Sarpi says talks at Worms were broken off after Eck and Melanchthon had spoken for three days. The emperor referred the rest to the Diet in Ratisbon.
calledBy: Charles V called the Diet and was there in person (Sarpi; Calvin). Calvin says the emperor was allowed to choose the speakers. Pallavicino says the Diet handed the choice back to him, and he named them with the legate taking part. The pope sent Cardinal Gaspar Contarini as legate at the emperor's request (Sarpi; Pallavicino).
attended: The six. Calvin and Pallavicino give the same names. For the Catholics: Julius Pflug, John Gropper of Cologne and John Eck. For the Protestants: Philip Melanchthon, Martin Bucer and John Pistorius.
Pallavicino says two presidents were named, Granvelle, the emperor's minister, and Frederick the Palatine, the Elector's brother. Six hearers were assigned, most of them officials of various princes.
Calvin says the Protestants asked, at his request, for a greater number of witnesses to be present.
The legate was Contarini. Calvin says the bishop of Modena, son of Jerome Morone, was sent separately as nuncio.
At the Diet. Calvin's letter of 28 March lists princes arriving, among them 'the two Bavarians', Frederick the Palatine, the Landgrave and the archbishop of Mainz.
He also names envoys of Venice, England, Portugal and France, and many bishops. The elector of Saxony stayed away and sent ambassadors.
Foxe says Henry VIII sent the bishop of Winchester and Sir Henry Knivet as joint ambassadors. The emperor was 'then at a diet or council at Ratisbon'.
Calvin came from Strasbourg as a deputy to the Diet. He was not one of the six. Pallavicino notes him too, 'di picciol nome' until then.
Peter Faber writes that he went to Ratisbon in January 1541, where the imperial diet was held. No held line puts him in the talks.
No count of those present is held, and no list of names.
decided: No act of the colloquy is held. What follows is told by Calvin and by the two historians, Sarpi and Pallavicino.
The Book. Pallavicino says the emperor had Granvelle carry a book to the legate. Granvelle said pious and learned men had written it.
It was woven largely from Scripture and the Fathers, in twenty-two chapters, Pallavicino says. Contarini found more than twenty places to correct, and Gropper corrected them without a word against.
Found free of error in the papal theologians' view, the book was put to the six at the emperor's command (Pallavicino). Sarpi calls it 'the Book of the Concord'.
Original sin and free will. Calvin wrote on 11 May that they agreed on original sin 'without any difficulty'. On free will, drawn from Augustine, they did not depart from the Protestant view.

Justification. Calvin says the debate here 'was more keen'. At length a formula, 'on receiving certain corrections, was accepted on both sides.' He sent Farel a copy, which the edition does not print.
Pallavicino says the parties agreed the articles on justification, faith, works, bishops and baptism. The legate reserved the pope's approval.
The Church. Calvin says they agreed on its definition but not on its power, and so left that article out.
The Lord's Supper. 'There stood the impassable rock which barred the way to farther progress,' Calvin wrote. The Protestants rejected transubstantiation.
Pallavicino says the first dissent was the Eucharist. The Lutherans began by refusing the word transubstantiation, as one the ancient Fathers did not use.
Melanchthon drew up a written statement for the Protestants, Calvin says. When it was given to Granvelle, it 'was rejected with harsh expressions'.

Later articles. On the saints, the pope's primacy and the Church's authority, Calvin writes, 'we could come to no agreement.' Sarpi lists five disputed articles, among them penance, the hierarchy and single life.
The emperor thanked the six and referred the whole to the estates, with the book and the articles (Calvin).
The recess. Sarpi says that on 28 July the emperor remitted the colloquy to a general council, a national synod or a diet. Failing a council, a diet would meet within eighteen months.
Pallavicino says the recess imposed the agreed articles until a council in Germany. The emperor said the legate had promised one; Pallavicino says Contarini had always refused a council there.
Calvin wrote on 3 August that all had been referred 'to an Universal Council, or, at least, to a National one'.
outcome: 'The whole plan of pacification passed off in smoke,' Calvin wrote. Yet he judged that 'the adverse party' had received 'no slight wound'.
Pallavicino says none of it took effect. The attacks did not stop, no council met in Germany, and neither party received the articles.
Eck had missed the last sessions with fever, Pallavicino says. He then wrote a sharp confutation of the book, and his two Catholic colleagues answered with an apology.

Rome. Paul III's bull of 1542 says the Diet called on him to tolerate certain Protestant articles until a council. Neither Catholic truth nor the Apostolic See's dignity, it says, would let him yield this.
Instead he chose to call for a council 'as soon as possible', the bull says. It names the diet of Ratisbon as the place where he proposed a council 'especially and finally'.
Sarpi, hostile to the papal court, also says the Diet moved the pope to work for a council. Pallavicino denies it.
Contarini under suspicion. Sarpi says he was 'much Caluminated in the Court of Rome', suspected of leaning to Lutheranism. Pallavicino says many in Rome blamed him as too cold against the Lutherans.
Pallavicino says Reginald Pole wrote to console him, and the pope received him warmly at Lucca.

Metz. The Histoire ecclésiastique says citizens there heard of the articles concluded at Ratisbon that year. They asked their magistrates for free exercise of religion under the Diet's resolution, and were refused.

The censors. The Spanish index of 1559 forbids works written against the imperial diet held at Ratisbon in 1541. The Roman index of Clement VIII still lists books against that diet, with no year (Reusch's edition).

record.witness: Calvin's letters from Ratisbon and Strasbourg, 19 February to 3 August 1541 (Bonnet's edition, English)
record.note: A Protestant deputy at the Diet, not one of the six. He reports the Protestant speakers from inside their side. The Latin originals are not held; the notes are Bonnet's.

record.witness: Peter Faber, Memoriale and his letter from Ratisbon of 12 May 1541 (Latin)
record.note: A Jesuit at the Diet, outside the talks; Catholic side. His Spanish letter of 12 March reaches us only as the MHSI editors quote it.

record.witness: Paul III, bull calling the Council of Trent, 1542 (Waterworth's English)
record.note: An act of the papacy, not of the colloquy: the pope's own account of the Diet a year later. Curia side. No Latin text is held.

record.witness: Paolo Sarpi, History of the Council of Trent (Brent's English, 1676)
record.note: A Venetian Servite friar, theologian to Venice in its quarrel with Pope Paul V; hostile to the papal court. Our scanned copy is damaged at several points.

record.witness: Sforza Pallavicino SJ, Istoria del Concilio di Trento (1664)
record.note: A Jesuit writing against Sarpi; for the papal court. He cites Contarini's letters, which are not held.

record.witness: Foxe, Acts and Monuments, with the 1837 editors' notes; the Histoire ecclésiastique attributed to Beza
record.note: Protestant histories. Foxe gives the English embassy at the Diet; the Histoire ecclésiastique gives the petition at Metz.

record.witness: F. H. Reusch, edition of sixteenth-century indexes of forbidden books (1886)
record.note: Later official lists of the Spanish Inquisition and of Rome, in a modern edition. They show writings against the Diet still banned decades later.

record.witness: J. Waterworth, historical essay in The Canons and Decrees of the Council of Trent (1848)
record.note: English Catholic. He says the colloquies of 'the years 1541-42' 'ended in nothing but disappointment'.

traditions.name: The Tridentine Church
traditions.note: The legate Contarini and the Catholic speakers Pflug, Gropper and Eck (Calvin; Pallavicino). The pope then refused to tolerate the agreed articles until a council (the 1542 bull).

traditions.name: Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations
traditions.note: Melanchthon and Pistorius sat with Bucer for the Protestants (Calvin). Sarpi says the Protestant estates would accept no council where the pope and his ministers judged.

traditions.name: The Reformed Cities - Zurich & Geneva
traditions.note: Calvin came as a deputy, serving Geneva's church 'as well as that of Strasbourg' (his letter of 19 February). He spoke at the Protestants' own meeting on the Supper.

traditions.name: The Society of Jesus
traditions.note: Faber went to the Diet, gave the Exercises to Spanish, Italian and German nobles, and made his profession at Ratisbon (his Memoriale).

traditions.name: The English Reformation & Elizabethan Settlement
traditions.note: Henry VIII's ambassadors attended the emperor at the Diet (Foxe; Calvin). No held line puts them in the talks.

people.name: Charles V
people.part: Emperor; called the Diet, chose the six and charged them; referred the whole to the estates and issued the recess (Calvin; Sarpi)

people.name: Gaspar Contarini
people.part: Cardinal and papal legate; read the Book and asked for corrections (Pallavicino); suspected in Rome afterwards (Sarpi; Pallavicino)

people.name: The bishop of Modena, son of Jerome Morone
people.part: Nuncio; with Contarini in reading the Book (Pallavicino). Calvin calls him 'altogether sanguinary'

people.name: Granvelle
people.part: The emperor's minister; brought the Book to the legate and presided (Pallavicino). Melanchthon's statement 'was rejected with harsh expressions' when presented to him; his reply 'cut off all hope' (Calvin)

people.name: John Gropper
people.part: Catholic speaker, archdeacon of Cologne; the legate and nuncio saw he wrote the Book (Pallavicino)

people.name: John Eck
people.part: Catholic speaker; fell ill during the talks (Calvin); later wrote a confutation of the Book (Pallavicino)

people.name: Philip Melanchthon
people.part: Protestant speaker; drew up the written statement on the Supper (Calvin)

people.name: Martin Bucer
people.part: Protestant speaker; with Melanchthon drew up formulas on transubstantiation that Calvin would not accept

people.name: John Pistorius
people.part: Protestant speaker; left out when Granvelle told the other four to confer alone (Calvin)

people.name: John Calvin
people.part: Deputy from Strasbourg; spoke in Latin at the Protestants' meeting on the Supper; our main eyewitness

people.name: Peter Faber
people.part: Jesuit at the Diet, outside the talks; wrote from the city on 12 May, and on 12 March as the MHSI editors quote him

people.name: John Brentz
people.part: Present; fighting 'more earnestly against the wafer god' than anyone, Calvin says

people.name: The bishop of Winchester
people.part: Henry VIII's ambassador at the Diet (Calvin; Foxe)

people.name: Martin Luther
people.part: Not present; one of the princes of Anhalt was sent to him secretly, Calvin says. His answer is not held

people.name: Paul III
people.part: Not present; sent the legate and refused to tolerate the articles; told the story in his bull of 1542

people.name: Reginald Pole
people.part: Not present; wrote to console Contarini afterwards (Pallavicino)

uncertain: None of the colloquy's own papers is held: not the Book, not the agreed article on justification, not the recess. Calvin's letters from the city stand in for them, with the rival histories of Sarpi and Pallavicino.

Melanchthon's and Bucer's own words on the talks are not held. They reach us through Calvin, on their side, and through Pallavicino, who calls the Protestants heretics. Luther's answer to the envoy is not held.
The crosses. Calvin calls Contarini legate 'from the Pope, who has distributed so many crosses for us at his first entrance'. The grammar lets 'who' be the pope.
But 'his first entrance' and the tired arm fit the legate, whose entry into the city Faber reports. The English is the 1858 translation; Calvin's Latin is not held.
The legate's entry on 12 March rests on Faber's Spanish letter as the MHSI editors quote it. The edition they cite is not held.
The legate's powers. Sarpi says Contarini excused the pope for not giving full power, since deciding matters of faith cannot be delegated. Pallavicino says Sarpi stumbles badly at the first step.
Pallavicino says the instruction's first chapter gave the legate no power to dispense the Church's laws and rites. Neither the instruction nor Contarini's letters are held.

Whether justification was truly agreed. Calvin says the formula kept 'the substance of the true doctrine'. Pallavicino says Rome found its words ambiguous. The pope told the legate to approve nothing not plainly Catholic. The Jesuit Faber, writing from the city on 12 May, does not name the talks. He says the business of the faith went forward 'valde ambigue', very doubtfully, so that he and his readers trust in God alone.
Who rejected the articles. Pallavicino says the Catholic princes, barons and bishops refused them as ambiguous, while most deputies of the Catholic cities wanted them accepted.
Sarpi says the bishops rejected the Book outright, and the other electors and Catholic princes did not side with them. The two agree on the bishops and differ on the princes.
Who wrote the Book. Only Pallavicino tells it. The legate and nuncio saw from various signs that Gropper was the author. Eck suspected 'il Vicelio', a man he hated.
What the Diet proved. Sarpi says it showed the Protestants they could win nothing where the pope's ministers had a part. Pallavicino calls this plainly false.
Sarpi also says the Diet moved the pope to work for a council. Pallavicino denies it, saying the pope had long sought one. The 1542 bull links the Diet to the council.
Contarini's written answer. Sarpi says it was no clearer than the ancient oracles. Pallavicino says everyone can feel how clear it was.
His welcome in Rome. Pallavicino charges Sarpi with saying the pope received him badly. The held English Sarpi says he 'gave absolute Satisfaction'; Pallavicino may be answering another text.
Sarpi's list of disputed articles does not name the Eucharist. It sits beside a gap in our scanned copy, so the silence may be loss.
The envoy to Luther. Calvin says 'the Marquis of Brandenbourg' sent one of the princes of Anhalt. He names neither man, and no held source of the time does.
The recess date, 28 July, is Sarpi's. Pallavicino dates a consistory to the day after the recess, but our copy is too damaged there to read the day.
A second colloquy met at Regensburg in 1546 (Sarpi; a letter from the city of 31 January 1546, in the MHSI edition). It is a separate event.
